note: Three problems chosen so that reasoning quality can differ even when the final answer agrees. Each carries a stable id, an exact expected answer, and the trap a plausible-but-wrong route falls into.

problems.title: Two pipes and a leak
problems.question: Pipe A alone fills a tank in 6 hours. Pipe B alone fills the same tank in 4 hours. A drain at the bottom empties a full tank in 9 hours. All three are opened at once on an empty tank. How many hours does it take to fill the tank? Give the answer as a fraction in lowest terms.
problems.why_this_problem: One clean derivation: the net rate is 1/6 + 1/4 - 1/9 = 11/36 of a tank per hour, so the time is the reciprocal. The common wrong route adds and subtracts the TIMES (6 + 4 - 9) instead of the rates. A model can also invert only at the very end and still narrate the reciprocal step incorrectly, which is a reasoning fault the final answer alone would never reveal.

problems.title: The second-largest divisor
problems.question: A positive integer n has exactly 8 positive divisors. The second-largest divisor of n is 21. Find n.
problems.why_this_problem: The second-largest divisor of n is n/p where p is the smallest prime factor, so n = 21p. Only p = 2 keeps 21 as the second-largest and gives 8 divisors, so n = 42. A model that simply guesses 42 because 42 = 21 x 2 lands on the right number without establishing why p = 2 or checking the divisor count. Correct answer, unjustified reasoning - which is the whole point of Part II.

problems.title: Lattice points under a line
problems.question: Let S be the set of ordered pairs of integers (x, y) with 1 <= x <= 20 and 1 <= y <= 20 such that 3x + 4y is divisible by 7. How many pairs are in S?
problems.why_this_problem: Reduce 3x + 4y = 0 (mod 7) to x = y (mod 7), then count. The range 1..20 is NOT a multiple of 7: residues 1..6 occur three times but residue 0 occurs only twice, so the count is 6*3^2 + 2^2 = 58, not 7*3^2 = 63. The near-miss 63 is exactly what careless counting produces, so judges have something real to disagree about.

dataset.name: AI-Math Workshop Problem Set
dataset.summary: Three problems written for this workshop. Deliberately NOT a public benchmark: a competition set that predates the models is contaminated, and one that postdates them is a moving target that cannot be re-run next year. These three are fixed, versioned, and chosen so that a model can reach the right answer by an invalid route — which is the whole point of Part II.
selection_criteria: Not arithmetic. Each needs a derivation a judge can score as valid or not.
Each has a specific plausible-but-wrong route that lands on a near-miss or, worse, on the right answer.
Solvable in a workshop without specialised mathematics.
Exact answers — a fraction or an integer, never a decimal approximation.
dataset.verification: Every answer was verified by brute force in Python before anything was built on it. Two of the three answers were WRONG in the first draft and the brute-force check caught both. That check is reproduced on this page.
dataset.answer_format: Each problem declares an exact expected answer plus the alternative spellings that mean the same value. The grader normalises presentation (LaTeX, $, thousands separators) and compares exact rationals — it never accepts a decimal approximation of a fraction.
dataset.licence: CC BY 4.0, with the rest of the workshop materials.
dataset.swapping_it_out: Replace problems/problems.json with the same shape and everything downstream follows: the loader, the matrix, the judge rotation and the website all read problem ids from that one file.
